articles.title: Attackers Tampered with AOMEI Backupper's Update Servers for Minutes to Deliver a Backdoor
articles.summary:
Attackers repeatedly changed the files that AOMEI Backupper fetches from the vendor's own update servers, in windows of five to ten minutes at a time between May and July 2026, so that any copy of the Windows backup program that checked for an update during one of those windows would download and run a backdoor.
Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant, and ManageEngine's Threat Analysis Lab, which disclosed the campaign this week, say AOMEI has reported fixing its servers, but that fix does not remove the backdoor from machines that were already hit.
AOMEI Backupper is Windows backup and disk-cloning software made by AOMEI Technology, a vendor registered in Hong Kong. Like the company's remote-desktop tool AnyViewer, it runs background services that regularly check AOMEI's servers over HTTPS for software updates and promotional pop-ups.
Two files drive that check. One, down_html.ini, names the update package to download and the checksum the program uses to verify it. The other, Notifycfg.ini, tells the pop-up service what to display and what to run.
The program does not cryptographically verify either file, and the checksum that is supposed to prove the download is genuine sits inside the same unsigned file that names it.
Nothing in the software was exploited. There was no vulnerability, and no user action was needed beyond having the program installed and running, according to ManageEngine's lab. The attacker only had to change two text files on the server for a few minut…

articles.title: Researchers Demonstrate OpenBSD Root Exploit Chaining 37-Year-Old Shared-Memory Bug
articles.summary:
A local privilege escalation exploit published today gains root on OpenBSD 7.9 by chaining a roughly 37-year-old integer overflow with a separate kernel flaw, bypassing OpenBSD's KARL kernel-address randomization and its SMAP and SMEP hardware protections. Security firm Calif, which found and reported the flaws, published a detailed writeup and full proof-of-concept code after OpenBSD shipped patches for both issues in September.
The integer overflow in the shmat(4) attach function was fixed in errata 018, shipped September 14 as a reliability fix. The reference-counting use-after-free that completes the chain was fixed separately in errata 026, shipped September 30 as a security fix.
Both are available through syspatch and cover all architectures. OpenBSD 7.8 also received the integer-overflow fix.
The integer overflow, the entry point for the full chain, is classified as a reliability fix, not a security fix.
No CVE has been assigned for either flaw as of publication. There is no evidence that the vulnerabilities have been used in attacks.
The shared-memory attachment counter shm_nattch is defined as a signed 16-bit short with a maximum value of 32,767 in original BSD sources dating to 1988. OpenBSD inherited the type and never widened it.
The exploit maps 127 shared-memory segments and forks 259 processes, pushing the counter past its maximum and wrapping it to −32,643. A race condition then triggers a use-after-free: the corrupted reference count causes the kernel to free…

articles.title: MALFEX npm Package 'imgdecode' Hides Shellcode Loader in Windows Native Addon
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers have discovered a malicious npm package that's part of a recently disclosed software supply chain attack campaign dubbed MALFEX.
The package, named "imgdecode," was uploaded to the package registry on September 30, 2026, by a user named "malfexteste8." It has been downloaded 979 times as of writing and is still available on npm as of writing. The latest version of the package is 1.0.3.
"The npm package imgdecode hides a malicious loader in a compiled Node.js addon," SafeDep said. "Its nine-line JavaScript file loads a Windows dynamic-link library (DLL). When a Node.js program calls require('imgdecode') from a Windows console, the DLL attempts to download encrypted shellcode from GitHub. It decrypts the response and injects the result into a new dllhost.exe process."
First documented by both Checkmarx and CloudSEK, MALFEX is the name assigned to a long-running campaign in which an unknown threat actor has been publishing malicious packages to npm since August 6, 2023, with an aim to compromise Windows systems. These packages were published across five npm publisher handles: malfexkkj, malfex_user, malfexteste2, malfexteste3, malfexteste4.
Of the eight identified packages, three were found to act as a loader for Overlord RAT, while three others ("cdn-img-fetch," "img-to-native," and "native-runner") worked together to download and run a Node.js stealer. articles.title: Just when we thought targeted ads couldn't get any worse, these were found serving malware
articles.summary:
Just when we thought targeted ads couldn't get any worse, these were found serving malware
Al Jazeera journalists were infected
- Researchers uncovered a zero-click spyware campaign delivered through online advertisements, requiring no user interaction
- Journalists’ devices were infected with surveillance malware capable of stealing data, messages, audio, and video
- Investigation linked the operation to Israeli firms tied to ad-tech infrastructure and commercial spyware
Imagine this: You’re a journalist. You get to work, log into your computer, and go about your daily activities. While browsing the internet, you see an ad for earbuds. You don’t click the ad, you don’t even view it with interest. You just get it served, much like any other ad on the internet, and scroll away to continue with your day.
But the moment the ad was served, through it your computer was infected with a powerful infostealer. The malware harvested all sorts of sensitive data, including files, documents, cookies, bookmarks, even saved credentials. It captured your keystrokes, took screenshots while you were working, and was even able to use your microphone and camera to record you while you were working.
Email messages, as well as instant messages shared through a wide range of platforms, were picked up and exfiltrated, as well.
